en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
*Sūrassatīnīti*:
The First Part.
From the mouth of the Blessed One, beautiful fragrant lotuses emerged as verses of homage.
With a mind full of faith, I pay homage to the supreme poet who has been born;
being requested, I shall compose [this work].
By a skillful royal counselor,
by name Santena,
[was taught] this policy that brings welfare to the world.
Beholding this treatise, which is adorned with ornaments,
provided with instructions, and named *Svarassati*,
may the peaceful ones look upon it.
Resembling a tree of Mañjuśrī,
always full of various instructions,
they are ever skilled in their own true welfare.
Generosity and gratitude, and truth—
these two are indeed the essence of the world.
The worlds also endure because of them;
they have made the kingdom their own.
And the crows and the wicked in the world—
Always becoming defiled,
they destroy their own desirable qualities;
they are indeed the enemies of the world.
The jackal is among the beasts,
while the crow is among the birds;
they are enemies without cause.
Just as fishermen are the constant enemies of fish,
so are the wicked the constant enemies of virtuous and noble people.
Worthy sirs, cultivate glory,
for prosperity has its root in glory;
it is through glory that people shine in this world.
Fortune brings about all success;
falsehood creates darkness in the world,
while truth is the maker of light.
"By one who is being tormented it is suffering;
by one who has attained truth it is happiness"—
this is easy for jackals to understand.
And the cry of birds,
O King— the cry of humans is even more difficult to discern than that.
Envy is like the fire at the end of an aeon,
burning away all prosperity;
sympathetic joy is like a cloud at the end of an aeon.
One establishes all forms of excellence,
just as unstable pillars erected upon a heap of chaff.
In the same way, the activities of those with monkey-like minds are fickle in their course.
A monkey-mind is like the dye of turmeric; it is unstable.
O dear one, do not associate with such a man who is devoid of passion,
even if he were to be a non-human being.
7. [Ka] A female parrot with flower-like beak and variegated wings,
intoxicated by her own beauty;
He moved from flower to flower;
he had no home and no social gathering. [Kha]
Though the female cricket is ill-favored in color,
she prevails through unity and effort;
do not be like the flower-sucker.
Just as dogs, playing together and delighting in one another,
might die while at play.
Having seen the food thrown away,
those who were hostile and harmful acted quickly;
even some people now did likewise.
Though they were once united and delighted with one another,
they now cause harm for the sake of wealth;
woe to those who quickly become enemies!
In spring, winter, and summer,
the palmyra trees do not change; likewise,
people who are peaceful and firm in mind remain the same.
Unshaken amidst pleasure and pain,
just as when a lathe is spinning,
the pivot remains perfectly still.
Just as a person who is paralyzed lies on the ground,
so too do those people;
they are unable to make him rise up.
For people are subject to time;
they are even able to pierce a diamond.
Therefore, time is of priceless value.
12. [Ka] For the Ka-plant is long-lasting,
the sārasāra is fragrant;
But the *simbali* tree, though it may be long-lived,
is indeed sapless and devoid of pith. [Kha]
Likewise, some people in the world are long-lived and very substantial,
while others are pithless like mere sapwood.
Even for a long time, like cattle,
both benefit and harm are lost upon him who goes away.
For one whose heart is like stone,
the designation "he lives" is in vain;
his faith is fruitless.
Even conversation is pointless;
one should not seek to associate with them,
just as a man or a woman would not with a eunuch.
Indeed, one should perform respectful conduct as long as friendship exists;
for respectful conduct [is required] even toward a good friend.
And there is the deception of deceit;
gradually, like sugarcane at the tip,
the flavor becomes sweeter.
Just so in this world, there is the good friend,
but the bad friend is not like him;
he is a refuge from the terror of sorrow.
One should desire the three syllables "Su-mi-tta" as a vessel for trust and joy,
a jewel among jewels.
For a husband and wife who are good friends,
each other's face is a mirror;
they share joy in happiness and sorrow in suffering.
Like reflections in a mirror—
how indeed can the hearts of those women who cry out so sweetly [be anything but cruel]?
Those who, while their own master is suffering,
desire happiness for themselves,
having made a shelter for themselves—
Having cast pride behind him,
the wise man should hold fast to his own welfare;
for folly is the destroyer of one's good.
Maintaining mindfulness while walking,
one should place faith behind;
the wise person does not hastily believe.
For one who has swift faith is slow in action.
In the forest there are many logs of wood;
red sandalwood is difficult to find.
So too, many people exist in the world,
but a person worthy of sacrifice is very difficult to find.
[They are like] grass, sticks, and foliage.
As a forest is consumed by dry wood,
so is the world consumed by people who are such as these, devoid of essence.
During the three months of the rains,
gladdened by their meritorious deeds,
those ancients dwelt in happiness.
Those who call themselves followers of the Buddha's teaching made that forest fragrant with the scent of musk.
In that way, by that virtuous and glorious person,
the kingdom was made like a body pierced at its vital points, destined for momentary destruction.
Virtues endure until the end of the aeon;
for lions and tigers, however,
there is never a gathering together.
In the same way, for those with tiger-like minds,
their own kind is a source of destruction;
even what is good for them is not good.
But he who does what is harmful for many people, though he may be mostly good,
is indeed called "good."
Even in the Bahūdaka ocean,
there would be no water left to drink;
yet in a small pit dug in the ground, there is plenty.
There is much delicious water here.
Do not open [the door] too quickly,
lest you be subject to blame or praise.
For the mouth is the gateway to your speech;
you should keep it closed at all times.
Do not open it too quickly.
The sight of you is dear to us;
for the gain of a loved one is slow,
while the gain of wealth is swift.
For the non-commencement of actions is the first characteristic of wisdom; [but] for one who has commenced,
reaching the conclusion is [the mark].
This is the second characteristic of intelligence:
one who does not examine their own actions and who acts with hasty impulsiveness.
Those deeds burn me, like hot food brought to my mouth;
they are fruitless and end in misery.
A wise person should not undertake actions that are censured by the people or those that are impossible to accomplish.
For those who fear great opposition,
who are suspicious at every step,
and who long for the doctrines of others—
Prosperity goes far away.
One should not fear what is merely spoken;
the world is the domain of sound.
But he who is terrified by mere sounds is like a wild deer wandering in the forest.
Of two handfuls of rice...
The distinction is clearly evident:
even when cooked, rice is succulent,
whereas parched grain is tasteless and harsh.
The rice grain is oily and flavorful;
thus it is known in the world.
A creeper clinging to a castor-oil plant—
Does it grow according to its strength?
Relying on a great sal tree,
it grows having reached a vast height.
For loving-kindness breaks down boundaries and destroys partiality;
through partiality, there is suffering.
One who has abandoned [faults] dwells in happiness.
Wisdom is the ornament of men when it is applied to its proper place.
A crest-jewel is not worn on the feet,
nor are sandals placed upon the head;
the wise desire that one should stand with upraised arms.
Freedom from curiosity regarding ministers,
moderation in food and drink,
and wisdom when a matter arises.
For negligence is darkness in the world;
Time is a terrifying thief;
the body-house has many openings.
Time is the thief that steals;
for Time’s slave is fickle,
while the master of Time is steadfast.
The power of time completely overcomes the power of the kingdom;
some utterly squander their wealth.
Some are black and many-eyed;
among them, those that are black, destructive,
terrifying, and triple-fanged are the most fearsome.
The king should work for the welfare of the kingdom,
and the people indeed for the welfare of the king;
the outcaste should seek his own welfare.
Indeed, one who causes harm is to be blamed.
One should not neglect one's own welfare for the sake of another’s,
even if that other’s interest is great.
To whomsoever a favor has been done,
one should return that favor again;
from that, one should discern the benefit.
One who is grateful is rare in this world.
Perhaps some people here have said that truth indeed exists.
A piece of wood that has washed ashore is better than even a man who is well-born, compassionate,
and possessed of his own wisdom.
One makes the wood precious;
likewise, a person who honors themselves becomes precious and esteemed by the world.
Just as iron, being of little value,
cuts through gold which is of great value,
so too in this world does one devoid of virtue [overcome] one possessed of virtue.
Alakkhī and Siri likewise;
this is the second section of the Sūrasaṃtī.
Wealth has two functions:
it raises the wealthy high and lowers the poor in this world.
By that [action] one gathers that wealth;
the wheel of time turns constantly and swiftly, unobstructed.
From that [unit of time], there arise the hour, the day, the month, and the year;
one should never make peace with an enemy.
At times he creates fear;
even well-heated water can indeed extinguish a fire.
For he who abandons his natural state and returns again to a modified state,
by way of his own inherent nature and form—
He undergoes a complete transformation,
like a lizard that has become a crocodile,
or like a woman who has entered the house of a man.
Having gained their wings,
they fly up like ants from an anthill;
once emerged, they go to their death.
Rising up, they have gone forth;
one should give everything dear to him,
with a mind that holds all as dear.
But the wise one with a mind of faith,
though stumbling while walking,
is able to leap a fathom’s length.
For he who was then [the king] Mahussāha,
through lack of effort, lost what was half-burnt;
among them, Anussāha was praised for his lack of effort.
Great exertion is suffering in the world;
lack of exertion is always happiness.
He who does not endure what is difficult to bear—
The life of a householder is difficult to endure;
when, then, shall he in this world obtain that which is easy, pleasant, and effortless?
For he would make manifest even that which is painful and difficult to do;
such a person is priceless in the world.
By means of providing clothing, food,
and other necessities, he performs that highly precious deed which is conducive to the welfare of the world.
They do not break even by the wind;
like bamboos, reeds, and rushes,
they do not go against the wind.
When should one live among people in such a way?
When there is no support for one who looks ahead or behind.
Extraordinary energy arises;
at that time, one becomes one's own refuge.
A lion [seizes] its moment, as a rat [seizes] its hole.
Filled with fragments of stone,
he may suffer the breaking of his claws,
or else become a mouse that eats fruit.
Blind people, lost on the path,
perceive what is not the path as the path;
likewise, those of poor wisdom are deluded.
They do not awaken to the true meaning of that.
There are two kinds of excellence of form: the lovely form and the heroic form.
One might desire a woman of lovely form,
or a man of heroic appearance;
for even fireflies burn brightly.
By the act of merely flapping their wings,
these lazy ones who sleep on do not fly;
so too are those people who perform such "work."
Like the contraction of a tortoise,
one should exercise restraint even in small matters; however,
when the time is right, one who knows policy should act.
Like a black snake that has risen up,
lions of lofty mind devour the remains of their prey.
Even if others do not urge them on,
one who desires growth should conduct themselves in that way;
for it is not merely by being "grown" that one has truly arisen.
The old age has been exhausted;
for one seeking welfare, new ninefold loving-kindness should be cultivated.
Whom do diseases not torment even with passion?
To whom do the faults of bad counsel not come?
Whom does a woman not honor, and whom does death not slay?
Established in what do sense objects no longer afflict?
(A Vasantatilakā verse: By means of a staff measuring a fathom’s length, [one remains unharmed].
I wade through the water with my arms;
whether it is shallow or deep,
in what is bottomless, I imagine it to be deep.
(Kha) Likewise, the dull-witted man, through his own perception,
considers the wise man to be shallow.
One does not know what is equal or unequal,
nor the great evil, nor the sharpness or dullness [of the faculties].
They converge upon a corrupt deed.
And here in this world,
they carry Death upon their heads while engaged in evil deeds;
they are deluded, associating with the deluded.
In this world, there are two kinds of association:
the straight and the crooked.
Only the straight is to be praised.
There was no other such gathering.
By this means, they lived together in harmony and mutual affection upon the great back wall.
(The Commentary on the Mahosadha Jātaka) The yūthikā flower is not blooming now.
Even when watered again and again,
it blooms when the proper time arrives;
in this way, you should maintain your energy.
The accumulation of wealth and the expenditure of wealth—
thus twofold indeed is the nature of wealth;
the method for the accumulation of wealth exists.
Not here, but in Dhanakkhepa,
is our motherless, fatherless,
aged, and fickle weaver.
One who knows the distinction should not speak with one whose mind is like a monkey and whose attachment is like turmeric,
if they desire their own success.
O dear one, do not associate with such a person who is devoid of passion,
even if he were to be non-human.
Virtues remain virtues when among those who recognize virtue,
but upon encountering one devoid of virtue, they become faults;
rivers that originate from pure waters remain so until they reach the sea.
Having reached the ocean, they become undrinkable;
they fashion a form of stone.
(Upajāti verse) They fashion a form of stone.
Just as a woodcutter repeatedly hews at a tree,
so too are fools fashioned by the exhortations of the virtuous.
From the *Cāṇakyanītilāgāthā*:
There are many faults in pampering,
but many virtues in disciplining.
Therefore, one should neither strike nor pamper one's son or pupil;
for regarding a friend who has passed away, [one should act with restraint].
Whoever would manifest hatred,
he indeed speaks of present hatred; this is known.
Those servants of the creeper who cling to its support—
by the destruction of that support, they too are destroyed.
They lie upon the ground like those without a protector,
pierced by the horns of hatred and trampled by the bits of pride.
Like a harmful cow, the fool causes fear in the world;
this world is afflicted from below to above.
He stood by Ujulekhā;
through his lies, he cast that world into unrighteousness.
A potter’s well-made vessel cannot be used by a noble person;
one should examine it with such a simile.
Even one who possesses personal prowess and the strength of others, though heroic,
cannot overcome thick darkness.
Just as rays cannot pierce through the world when it is thus deluded by intoxication,
they are unable to break through that intoxication.
To shine with the light of wisdom:
for the poor there is the misery of hunger,
and for the wealthy there is the calamity of disease.
And in the command over one's own wealth,
one should perceive the true nature of the world;
with the excellent enjoyment thus acquired, [one should live].
One who makes one's own life pure is the best by virtue of that life;
one who lives on filth is loathsome.
How indeed could he who does not perceive the distinction between a diamond and red flowers sell [the former]?
Or one might as well destroy a mountain by thinking it over with great effort,
as if one were a woodpecker.
That thought is indeed vain and foolish, like that of a weak woman who is thin in her middle;
for one who does not [strike] an enemy as soon as he is born—
One should bring even a disease to its subsistence; for by that very means,
even one of great strength, having reached full growth, is destroyed.
O you with mouths always dripping with saliva,
who eat the flesh of living beings—
of cats, tigers, and lions!
The mouths of men indeed utter many kinds of base, sharp, and harsh words.
They run about destroying [the crops],
by means of their livelihood-gaining work;
people are distressed because of that.
They wander with their faces turned away from the Dhamma.
What is worldly is easy to find in the world,
but that which pertains to the Teaching is indeed difficult to find.
He who, regarding it as difficult to find,
would throw away that fire-pit where he has found a firm footing— he would be the most foolish of fools.
Out of delusion, he went to help him;
then another, even more foolish,
entered the enclosure as his companion.
For a tiger pierced by a weapon indeed utters a harsh roar;
even so does one who has been struck by a band of good men.
The fool, pierced and agitated,
drinks his own blood;
the flies lick him from within with their proboscises.
People surround them on the outside,
and because of that, the public bites them.
For one who is destitute, the opportunity is rare.
The true Dhamma lasts for only a short time;
few would apply themselves to it,
even though much opportunity is available.
